item.title: Load shedding hits various areas of Dhaka at night
item.description:
Residents of various areas of the capital Dhaka experienced prolonged load shedding on Wednesday night. Many residents reported power outages around midnight.

Some areas experienced load shedding for one and a half to two hours, while others remained without electricity for more than an hour. The prolonged power cuts caused considerable discomfort for Dhaka residents amid the humid and oppressive heat.

Residents said there was no electricity between 9:00 pm and 1:30 am in Bashundhara Residential Area, parts of Eskaton Garden, Kazipara, Mouchak, Karwan Bazar, Panthapath, West Rajabazar, Lalmatia and the Krishi Market area of Mohammadpur.

Prothom Alo correspondents reported load shedding from various areas around midnight. At around 11:00 pm, one reporter went to Shewrapara and found that his home had no electricity. Power was restored there about an hour later.

A resident of Mouchak said that although transformer problems usually occur in the area, electricity normally returns within five to 10 minutes. However, power had still not returned after nearly 50 minutes on Wednesday night.

Severe suffering amid intense heat

Anika Tasnim, a resident of Bashundhara Residential Area, said her neighbourhood experienced more than an hour of load shedding around midnight. She said she had never experienced such prolonged load shedding in Dhaka at midnight before.

Anika said, “Yet my electricity bill has doubled compared with before. The load shedding at midnight is causing serious problems with my sleep.”

Rahat Ahmed, a resident of Kazipara and a journalist at a private television channel, said Wednesday night saw the longest period of load shedding he had experienced in his area in the past three years.

He said, “It has become difficult to sleep because of the intense heat and mosquitoes.” He urged the government to reduce mismanagement in the power sector and restore comfort to people’s lives.

Residents of Karwan Bazar, Panthapath, West Rajabazar and the Krishi Market area of Mohammadpur also reported power outages at night.

However, the situation was not the same across the capital. A resident said electricity supply remained normal in Mirpur-11 and the Journalist Residential area until 12:30 am. He said there was no electricity in the Bihari Camp area when he returned home at around 10:30 pm.

Load Shedding increase across the country

Load shedding has increased across the country as the ongoing gas shortage has reduced electricity generation. The country has experienced peak load shedding of more than 3,000 megawatts for several days. The highest level of load shedding on Wednesday was 3,382 megawatts.

Data from the Bangladesh Power Development Board (PDB) and Power Grid Bangladesh PLC (PGCB) showed that peak load shedding stood at 3,671 megawatts last Sunday.

It increased to 3,757 megawatts on Monday, before falling to 3,465 megawatts on Tuesday and 3,382 megawatts on Wednesday.

Sources at the PDB and Rural Electrification Board (REB) said the country recorded total load shedding of 3,592 megawatts at midnight on 11 August. At the same time, REB areas experienced 3,034 megawatts of load shedding.

Meanwhile, gas supplies have also declined. The country received 2.03 billion cubic feet of gas yesterday, Wednesday against demand of 3.8 billion cubic feet. Due to adverse weather conditions at sea, gas supplies from Summit’s floating LNG terminal have fallen below 100 million cubic feet.

State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam Amit told Prothom Alo on Wednesday that the gas supply shortage was disrupting electricity generation.

He said, “The government is making every possible effort to improve the power and gas situation.”

item.title: Bangladesh quick Hasan reduces Australia to 74-4 at lunch
item.description:
Bangladesh quick bowler Hasan Mahmud took two wickets on Thursday to reduce Australia to 74-4 at lunch after the hosts won the toss and chose to bat on the opening day of the first Test in Darwin.

Cameron Green fell on the last ball of the session for 13 leaving Steve Smith not out on seven at the other end, with wicketkeeper Alex Carey due in next.

Australia went into the Test with a full-strength team and were expected to have little trouble against a Bangladesh side that were well-beaten by a Cricket Australia XI in their only warm-up match.

But Bangladesh's opening bowlers were impressive early, with both Taskin Ahmed and Hasan keeping a disciplined line and length on a slow pitch.

Hasan troubled both openers, Travis Head and Jake Weatherald, and made the breakthrough with the score on 45 in the 12th over.

Weatherald, on 23, had a huge swipe at a ball outside off stump and only managed a thick edge to wicketkeeper Litton Das.

Hasan struck again soon after, Head chopping on for 22 to leave Australia 52-2.

Bangladesh then saw a huge opportunity go begging when Smith, on two, edged Ebadot Hossain to third slip where Tanzid Hasan spilled the chance.

Smith had a second escape next over when he got a thick edge off Taskin only for the ball to fly through a vacant third slip.

Marnus Labuschagne, on one, wasn't so fortunate.

He poked at an Ebadot ball outside off stump and edged to Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto at second slip, leaving Australia 61-3.

Green came in and played some big shots before chipping Taskin to short midwicket where Mushfiqur Rahim took an easy catch.

item.title: Bangladesh’s pace attack puts Australia under pressure in Darwin
item.description:
Bangladesh have made an impressive start to the first Test against Australia in Darwin, with their pace attack exploiting the conditions at Marrara Stadium to reduce the hosts to 64 for three after 19 overs.

Australia won the toss and elected to bat, with Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto leading a side featuring three fast bowlers and two spinners.

Taskin Ahmed and Hasan Mahmud opened the bowling for Bangladesh, and both immediately found movement and bounce from a pitch with a noticeable covering of grass.

Hasan was particularly impressive with the new ball, repeatedly troubling Australia’s openers with deliveries that moved both ways. His bowling was rewarded in the 12th over when Weatherald, after earlier being tempted by deliveries outside off stump, edged one through to wicketkeeper Litton Das. He departed for 23, with Hasan claiming his first wicket of the innings.

Hasan struck again in the 14th over, removing Travis Head for 22. Bowling around the wicket, he produced a good-length delivery that jagged back into the left-hander and struck the stumps. Steve Smith then came to the crease at No. 4.

Earlier, Ebadot Hossain had replaced Taskin as the first change in the ninth over and made an immediate impact. He twice beat Head with excellent deliveries and finished his opening over as a maiden. Bangladesh also reviewed an lbw appeal against Head from Ebadot’s fifth delivery, but the review did not overturn the on-field decision.

Hasan continued to keep Australia’s batters uncomfortable, particularly with the movement he generated from a good length. Weatherald was beaten again in the sixth over, while Head and Weatherald struggled to settle against Bangladesh’s disciplined pace bowling.

Australia reached 31 without loss after eight overs, with Weatherald on 14 and Head on 10. However, the pressure created by Bangladesh’s bowlers eventually produced wickets.

Smith was given a reprieve when Tanzid Tamim failed to hold a catch at third slip off Ebadot’s bowling in the 17th over. The ball came low off the bat but was within catching range, and dropping a batter of Smith’s calibre could yet prove costly for Bangladesh.

Ebadot then claimed his first wicket of the innings in the 19th over. Marnus Labuschagne could have left the second delivery of the over alone, but attempted to play it and edged the ball to Najmul at second slip. Labuschagne departed for one, continuing a difficult run of form. Ebadot celebrated the wicket with his trademark salute.

At that point, Australia were 64 for three after 19 overs, having lost three wickets for just 16 runs between 11.4 and 18.2 overs. The collapse was a reward for Bangladesh’s disciplined bowling in the right areas.

The opening phase of the Test had already demonstrated the importance of the surface. Before the match, Australian opener Travis Head described the pitch as looking hard with grass on it. Hasan’s third over provided early evidence of the assistance available to the fast bowlers, with the ball showing both movement and extra bounce. One delivery beat Weatherald’s bat comprehensively, while another caused Head to mistime his shot.

Bangladesh were without right-arm fast bowler Nahid Rana, who is unavailable for the series because of injury. Nevertheless, Taskin and Hasan gave the visitors a strong start with the new ball, while Ebadot maintained the pressure after coming into the attack.

The match is particularly significant for Bangladesh, as it marks their first Test on Australian soil in 23 years. Bangladesh last toured Australia for Tests in 2003, losing both matches by an innings. The two sides have since played four further Tests, all of them in Bangladesh.

Australia, meanwhile, are beginning a lengthy and demanding season with this match. Captain Pat Cummins said before the toss that his side had been looking forward to the contest, while Najmul said Bangladesh were proud to be in Darwin and eager to play.

The match also marks the return of Test cricket to Darwin after a 22-year absence. The unfamiliar conditions at Marrara Stadium mean the venue itself presents a challenge for Australia, despite the hosts' familiarity with Australian conditions.

Former Australia fast bowler Jason Gillespie, a familiar figure to Bangladesh supporters, carried the series trophy onto the field before the national anthems.

Gillespie scored an unbeaten double-century against Bangladesh in 2006 as a nightwatchman—the highest individual score by a nightwatchman in Test cricket. The match marks 20 years since that remarkable innings.

For Bangladesh, the immediate task is to maintain the pressure created by their fast bowlers. With Australia already three wickets down, the visitors have made an encouraging start to a Test that represents a significant moment in their cricketing history.

Teams

Bangladesh: Tanzid Hasan, Shadman Islam, Mominul Haque, Najmul Hossain (capt), Mushfiqur Rahim, Litton Das (wicketkeeper), Mehidy Hasan Miraz, Taijul Islam, Taskin Ahmed, Ebadot Hossain and Hasan Mahmud.

Australia: Jake Weatherald, Travis Head, Marnus Labuschagne, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Alex Carey, Beau Webster, Mitchell Starc, Pat Cummins (capt), Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood

item.title: Rising heat in Asia: The toll it takes on your organs
item.description:
Thirty-year-old Vaishnavi Sharma works at an advertising agency in Gurugram and travels nearly 90 kilometres daily to reach her office from her home in Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh, India. She says travelling doesn’t drain her as much as the heat does.
Detailing a recent incident, Sharma tells Asian Dispatch : “It was around 8:30 in the night, I left the office and reached the [Sikanderpur] metro station. By the time I reached, I felt drained because of the heat. I could not take the stairs or elevator. I had to sit there for five minutes and ask somebody to get me a bottle of water.”
Sharma says she has been travelling long distances for work for years but now the sun feels harsher and unbearable. “You can't sit without covering your face. Earlier, I was able to easily sit in an auto for a longer duration but now even if the temperature is comparatively lower, I feel I can't step out.”
Sharma also spoke about developing skin allergies, experiencing hair loss, and pigmentation around her face, hands, and feet due to the heat.
A 23-year-old student from Dhaka, Bangladesh, Fariha Tasnim, studies at the University of Asia Pacific (UAP). She says, “I have developed rashes on my body, I am unable to sleep at night because of the heat. My body feels dehydrated, and in some cases, when the heat becomes extremely intense, blister-like spots appear.”
Picture1
Fariha Tasnim, a 23-year-old student studying at University of Asia Pacific (UAP) in Dhaka in Bangladesh.
Tasnim spends nearly six hours on an average in the heat every day. She travels to her university to attend classes and then to the homes of the students she teaches. She mentions that going outside in the heat is unavoidable because of college and work.
Sharma and Tasnim’s experience highlight the impact heat has on people’s health. While these are anecdotes, studies also note that heat increases health risks such as heat strokes and makes non-communicable diseases such as diabetes and hypertension worse.
However, these cases are not limited to India or Bangladesh, the pattern is consistent across Asia.
According to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), Asia has warmed up faster than the global average in the recent decades.
It also accounted for 45% of the global heat-related deaths between 2000-2019.
So, why is Asia warming up so fast?
Gautam Menon, a professor of physics and biology at Ashoka University, said that the greater rise in temperature is because of the region’s larger landmass.
“The impacts of climate change are not uniform across the globe, even as there is a general increase in global temperatures. The large continental landmass of Asia means that higher temperatures can be sustained over longer periods, and Asia has warmed significantly faster than the rest of the world. The experience of heat depends on several local factors, among them [is] built urban environments, as cities in Asia increasingly urbanize”, Menon says.
Menon also explained how this heat puts a burden on the human body. “Extreme heat places increased demands on the body, calling on greater resources. Unless one is well hydrated, increased demands are placed on the kidneys, among other organs, while heat stress affects every organ in both direct and indirect ways.”
The heart
“To keep the body cool, blood-vessels will start dilating, and they become warmer. So, the sweating increases. Sweating is also a part of the body’s mechanism to cool down. Whenever there is sweating, there is a loss of salt and electrolytes from the body. It can cause a decrease in the total body water as well as the electrolytes. Now, suppose somebody is healthy, all these things are manageable. But when somebody who has got heart disease or is a patient of heart failure, or has blocked arteries, or high blood-pressure, this can cause issues with the heart.” - Dr Rahul Gupta, Director and Head of Cardiology and Structural Heart Program, Gleneagles Hospitals

A study published in 2022 said that “a 1°C increase in temperature was positively associated with cardiovascular disease-related mortality across all considered diagnoses. The overall risk of cardiovascular disease-related mortality increased by 2.1%.”
The brain
“The bad impact on the brain - especially for the neurological side - is that these heat waves can increase certain neurological disorders because the brain as well as the nerves are very sensitive to high core temperatures. It can damage the nerves, which are present in the brain as well as the spinal nerves. It can also damage the blood-brain barrier.” - Dr Puneet Agarwal, Vice-Chairman of Neurology, Max HealthCare
Dr Agarwal said that if the core body temperature goes beyond over 40°C or 104°F, then the nerves in the body and blood-brain barrier gets affected and damaged. This can lead to swelling in the nerves and brain.

Multiple studies have concluded that long-term exposure to extreme high temperatures can lead to cognitive decline.
The liver
“When the core [body] temperature goes above 40°C, it causes hepatocyte [damage], meaning liver cells damage and necrosis. There could also be dehydration. Dehydration would lead to reduced blood flow. That will cause an ischemia-reperfusion injury because of the sluggish flow or reduced flow.” - Dr Chetan Kalal, Associate Director, Hepatology and Liver Transplant, Gleneagles Hospital
Dr Kalal said that the liver is among the first organs to fail in these extreme heat conditions.
A research paper published in January 2026 also highlighted that the liver is one of the earliest organs to be damaged in case of a heat-induced multiple organ dysfunction syndrome. The paper said that the liver is particularly vulnerable to temperature fluctuations. Acute liver injury (ALI) and acute liver failure (ALF) are serious complications and are direct causes of patient death.
The kidneys
“People who have pre-existing hypertension, diabetes, chronic kidney disease or at risk of developing further worsening of kidney functions. This is because of the excess volume depletion due to profuse sweating causing further kidney injury. People who do not have any previous kidney problems also are at risk of developing acute kidney injury.” - Dr S Sathiyan, Senior Consultant, Nephrology, SIMS Hospital

A research paper published in March 2026 noted, “Multiple studies across diverse settings have shown increased hospital admissions for acute kidney injury on days of high ambient temperature and during heatwave.”
Who is most affected?
People who work outdoors during peak hours such as construction workers, farmers, and gig workers are the most vulnerable group to illnesses related to rising temperature. People with pre-existing medical conditions, elderly, children, and pregnant women also come under this category.
I met Yogendra Prasad, 33, who hails from Ayodhya, Uttar Pradesh, India works for a company that conducts surveys in Delhi. He travels everyday via bus to meet people and takes photographs of shops in Delhi to collect data for his company. Prasad says he faces difficulties in summers and sometimes experiences dizziness but he has to do his work.
Picture1
Yogendra Yadav, 33, carries a cloth over his head to protect himself from the heat. Photo: Shivansh Srivastava/Asian Dispatch
There are many more like Prasad.
Picture1
Pappu Yadav, 36, runs a paratha shop in Jasola Vihar, Delhi, in India. Photo: Shivansh Srivastava/Asian Dispatch
Dr Subarna Goswami, a public-health administrator based in West Bengal, argued that the construction workers, people working on the roads under the sun, and the working class are the “people who contribute the least to this global warming but are the worst victims.”
Sharma’s battle with heat and responsibilities don’t end with her work shift either. She mentioned that after completing work and reaching home, she cooks dinner for herself and her family. “I stand in the kitchen, even if there is ventilation, I have to stand in front of the gas. So again, I have to stand in heat. I don't think I am able to relax in the AC again until 11pm”, she says.
The future that lies ahead
Menon argues that given the pace of climate change, there is almost nothing that can be done over a short period of time.
"Given the pace of climate change, historical emissions, and the inertia of the climate system, there is almost nothing that governments can do that might make a difference over the short to intermediate term. Over the long term, over a century or more, an immediate reduction in emissions will have an impact, but it will again take a long time to stabilize. It should be an absolute priority to reduce carbon emissions to levels of about a century ago, through the use of renewables", Menon says.

item.title: The quiet geometry of a balancing act
item.description:
For weeks, speculation over Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's first foreign trip ran through Dhaka's political class with much intensity. India, Turkey, and the United Kingdom were all floated in turn, fed by nothing more than the silence of those who actually knew.
The travel date itself was disclosed only two days ahead of departure, and when the delegation was finally named, it was pointedly lean: No sprawling political entourage, only the relevant officials the visit required.
The destination was Kuala Lumpur, then Beijing, a pairing that answered the earlier guesswork with a kind of quiet deliberateness. The groundwork, it turned out, had been laid well before departure: Senior officials had made repeated visits to both capitals in the preceding months, and Bangladesh's presence at the World Economic Forum event meant that it was well planned from before.
And once underway, it turned into an argument -- the one this government has made its signature. " Shobar aage Bangladesh ," or "Bangladesh first." It is an easy phrase to print on a banner and a hard one to honour,, where slogans tend to die quiet deaths in the white space between diplomatic communiqués.
What this tour demonstrated is that the phrase was actually meant to be operative instead of just being ornamental. A foreign policy organized around the country's needs: Jobs, investment, market access, and the dignity of millions of Bangladeshis whose remittances keep the national ledger breathing.
Malaysia made plain sense as the opening stop. A major Muslim-majority Southeast Asian economy, home to a vast Bangladeshi workforce, and a gateway to the regional architecture Dhaka has long wished to enter the Asean in any format.
It also carried weight on a question closer to home: With more than a million Rohingya still sheltered in Cox's Bazar and no credible path to repatriation in sight, Malaysia's standing within the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) and its voice among Asean member states make its support worth courting.
The prime minister raised both threads with his counterpart, Anwar Ibrahim -- pressing for a labour corridor that manages demand transparently, defines requirements clearly, and safeguards the welfare of Bangladeshi workers rather than leaving them exposed to predatory recruitment.
Beyond labour, the two governments agreed to work towards a free trade agreement by 2027, and Malaysia lent its support to Bangladesh's aspiration to join the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and to secure Asean Sectoral Dialogue Partner status.
Then came China, and the elevation of the register that China always demands. The prime minister was received by the three powerful figures in the Chinese state - President Xi Jinping, Premier Li Qiang, and the chairman of the National People's Congress in Beijing.
Beijing voiced support for Dhaka's ambitions toward Brics and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, agreed a strategic dialogue between the two foreign ministers, and discussed within its capacity about the comprehensive management of the Teesta. Ahead of the visit, the government cleared the roughly Tk 4,189 crore infrastructure plan for the Chinese Economic and Industrial Zone in Anwara. The runway on which a hoped-for half a billion dollars of investment and a hundred thousand jobs are meant, in time, to land.
Dhaka did not conclude a free trade agreement with Beijing. It signed memoranda, framed the Teesta engagement as a matter of feasibility rather than strategic embrace, and ensured the communiqué stated plainly that the cooperation is directed at no third party. That restraint is not timid.
Four months earlier, Bangladesh signed an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States , which is a significant agenda. It lowered the reciprocal tariff on Bangladeshi exports and opened the prospect of zero-tariff treatment for garments made with American cotton, no small thing for the industry that is the spine of the economy.
That agreement also set boundaries: It provided that a preferential economic pact with a country Washington designates as "non-market" could place the tariff relief at risk. The balancing act, then, is not a rhetorical flourish about being friends with everyone. It is a real constraint, and the Beijing visit was calibrated precisely not to unsettle others whilst following what is best for the country.
It honoured the commitment to Washington and the welcome in Beijing, and it has continued to engage New Delhi in parallel, the prime minister having already received an invitation to visit.
A word of realism is owed, because analysis is not flattery. A communiqué is only a promissory note, not a delivered project, and Bangladesh's historic difficulty has never been signing agreements but absorbing them.
Vietnam sustains close ties with Washington and attracts vast Chinese investment at once, because it has built the institutional capacity to metabolize both. Our task is the same: To move faster, to lighten the bureaucratic weight that sits on ambition, and to ensure that a memorandum signed with fanfare becomes a factory that employs.
The Anwara zone has been long in the waiting; the labour corridor remains, for now, a principle rather than a passage. The gains of this tour are real, but they are options purchased and an option only has value when it is exercised.
So the verdict should be confident and clear-eyed at once. In a single tour, Tarique Rahman showed that Bangladesh can compose a sophisticated foreign policy sentence: Independent in its choices, plural in its partnerships, disciplined within real constraints, and answerable first to its own people's needs.
The next chapter is delivery. For “ Shobar aage Bangladesh” to mean everything its authors intend, the order must now hold in implementation as surely as it has held in diplomacy because a country that learns to put itself first abroad must also learn to deliver for itself at home.
Ashfaq Zaman is the founder of Dhaka Forum and a strategic international affairs expert.

item.title: When the waters recede, inequality remains
item.description:
The floodwater has disappeared from Satkania and Banshkhali. Roads are reopening, markets are slowly filling with customers again, and children are beginning to return to school. To many, the crisis is over.
But for the families I met during a recent visit to these flood-hit communities, the real struggle has only just begun.
Climate disasters do not affect everyone equally. They expose the inequalities that already exist -- between women and men, girls and boys, rich and poor, those with disabilities and those without, and between households with support and those left to cope alone.
The July flash floods in Chittagong were not just an environmental disaster; they were a stark reminder that vulnerability is deeply shaped by gender and intersecting social realities. Homes collapsed, crops were destroyed, roads disappeared under water, and access to healthcare, education, and safe drinking water was severely disrupted. Yet behind these statistics are stories that reveal what disaster truly looks like.
In Ilsha village of Banshkhali, I met Shifa, a 14-year-old girl who dreams of becoming an Army officer. When the flood struck, her family fled with nothing. Returning home, they found their mud house damaged and her schoolbooks buried beneath thick mud.
Her father is undergoing cancer treatment and fears he can no longer afford to keep her in school. The flood also coincided with her menstruation, leaving her without privacy or adequate facilities to manage it safely.
For many, the flood damaged a house. For Shifa, it threatened a future.
Climate disasters interrupt far more than infrastructure. They interrupt education, aspirations, and the life chances of adolescent girls. Every missed examination, every destroyed textbook and every financial setback pushes girls closer to dropping out of school or being married early.
In the Nolua Union of Satkania, Sadia showed me another face of vulnerability. As the head of her household and sole caregiver of her three-year-old child with a disability, she faced the flood entirely alone.
She carried household belongings to safety while caring for her child, managed without menstrual hygiene products by tearing pieces from an old saree, and developed painful skin infections after prolonged exposure to contaminated floodwater. Her husband works abroad but is seriously ill and unable to support the family financially.
Sadia's experience cannot be explained by gender alone. It is the intersection of gender, disability, poverty, and unpaid caregiving that placed her at far greater risk than others around her.
That is the essence of intersectionality. Disasters may strike an entire community, but they do not strike everyone with equal force.
The same pattern emerged in the story of Parvin Akter, a widow raising three daughters on her own. During displacement, one of her adolescent daughters started menstruating without access to sanitary materials or a private place to change.
After returning home, soaring food prices forced impossible choices between buying food, hygiene supplies and school materials. Poverty did not simply make recovery harder; being a female-headed household multiplied those challenges.
Older women faced another layer of exclusion. Shefali Rani Das, aged 60, described being trapped inside her flooded home because she could barely move through the water.
Cooking became impossible, toilets disappeared beneath floodwater, and damaged roads isolated her community. Without nearby emergency shelters or reliable assistance, surviving the flood depended largely on family members who could help her move.
Throughout the visit, one reality surfaced repeatedly but rarely appears in official damage assessments: Disasters dramatically increase women's unpaid care work.
Women cleaned mud-filled homes, searched for water, cooked under impossible conditions, cared for sick children and elderly relatives, repaired damaged houses and tried to restore some sense of normalcy -- all while carrying the emotional burden of holding families together.
Recovery begins long before humanitarian assistance arrives, and much of that recovery rests on invisible, unpaid labour performed by women.
The women and girls I spoke with rarely asked for sympathy. They asked for dignity.
They spoke about inaccessible toilets, the absence of menstrual hygiene materials, damaged schools, skin diseases caused by contaminated water, and the anxiety of not knowing how they would rebuild their lives.
As climate change intensifies, Bangladesh will experience more frequent and severe weather extremes. Whether these hazards become humanitarian disasters depends not only on rainfall or river levels but on how prepared we are to protect those facing multiple and overlapping vulnerabilities.
An intersectional approach must move from policy language to practice. That means prioritising female-headed households, adolescent girls, older persons, persons with disabilities, pregnant and lactating women, and caregivers in disaster preparedness and recovery.
It means designing accessible shelters, ensuring dignified menstrual hygiene management, expanding cash assistance, strengthening psychosocial support, and recognising and reducing women's unpaid care work as part of resilience building.
What gave me some hope in Satkania and Banshkhali were the people. Neighbours rescued one another before formal relief arrived. Families shared food with those who had none. Girls like Shifa still spoke confidently about becoming Army officers, teachers and professionals despite everything they had lost.
They do not need pity. They need policies that see them.
When the next flood comes -- and it will -- the greatest danger will not only be the rising water. It will be our failure to recognize that vulnerability is never one-dimensional, and that building resilience begins by putting those standing in the deepest water at the centre of our response.
Rowshon Akhter Urmee is a Gender Justice & Social Inclusion Specialist, Oxfam in Bangladesh.

item.title: Dhaka air quality moderate Thursday
item.description:
Dhaka ranked 23rd among the world’s cities with the worst air quality on Thursday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 79 at 9:05am.
According to the AQI scale, the capital’s air quality was classified as ‘Moderate’, indicating that it generally poses little or no risk to the general population, though unusually sensitive individuals may experience some health concerns.
Uganda’s Kampala topped the global pollution list with an AQI score of 196, followed by Kuching in the Malaysia with 187 and Lahore in Pakistan with 179.
An AQI reading of 101 to 150 is considered ‘unhealthy for sensitive groups’, while 151 to 200 is classified as ‘unhealthy’. A reading between 201 and 300 is considered ‘very unhealthy’, and anything above 301 is categorized as ‘hazardous’, posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides a daily indication of air quality by measuring the level of pollution and its potential impact on human health.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants — particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long faced serious air pollution problems, with air quality generally deteriorating during the winter months and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution contributes to around 7 million deaths worldwide every year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.description:
The nomination paper of Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) Chairman Colonel (retd) Oli Ahmad has been submitted as the candidate of the 11-party alliance led by the main opposition Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami for the presidential election.

Leaders of the 11-party alliance submitted the nomination paper on behalf of Oli Ahmad to the returning officer for the presidential election, Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) AMM Nasir Uddin at around 12:00 pm today, Thursday.

Jamaat Assistant Secretary General Hamidur Rahman Azad and National Citizen Party (NCP) Chief Coordinator Nasir Uddin Patwary submitted the nomination paper to the CEC. Central leaders of the 11-party alliance and several MPs were present at the time.

Leader of the opposition Jamaat Ameer Shafiqur Rahman signed as the proposer of Oli Ahmad’s nomination, while NCP MP Abdullah Al Amin signed as the seconder.

BNP collects two nomination papers for presidential election

According to the announced election schedule, nomination papers for the presidential election can be submitted from 10:00 am to 4:00 pm today. The nomination papers will be scrutinised on 16 August, while 18 August is the last day for withdrawal of nominations. Voting in the presidential election will take place on 20 August.

A sitting of parliament has been convened on 20 August for voting in the presidential election. Voting is held in the chamber of the Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban. Members of parliament are the voters in the presidential election, and the president is elected through their open vote.

item.title: Hasan takes 6-55 as Bangladesh bundle out Australia for 198
item.description:
Hasan Mahmud took a career-best 6-55 as Bangladesh bundled Australia out for 198 on the opening day of the first Test in Darwin on Thursday.

Mahmud led an impressive display by the visitors' seamers as Australia slumped to their lowest Test score against Bangladesh, their previous worst being 217 in Mirpur in 2017.

Hasan was the pick of the attack, but he was ably supported by fellow quicks Taskin Ahmed and Ebadot Hossain, who took two wickets apiece.

Steve Smith was the only Australian to offer any resistance, scoring 71, while the rest of the batsmen looked out of sorts against the disciplined attack.

After skipper Pat Cummins chose to bat on a perfect Darwin day, a full-strength Australia were expected to dominate a Bangladesh side who were well beaten by a Cricket Australia XI in their only warm-up match.

Hasan, who troubled openers Travis Head and Jake Weatherald in his opening spell, made the initial breakthrough in the 12th over with the score on 45.

Weatherald, on 23, had a huge swipe at a ball outside off stump and only managed a thick edge to wicketkeeper Litton Das.

Hasan struck again soon after, Head chopping on for 22 to leave Australia 52-2.

Bangladesh then saw a huge opportunity go begging when Smith, on two, edged Ebadot to third slip where Tanzid Hasan spilled the chance.

Smith had a second escape next over when he got a thick edge off Taskin only for the ball to fly through a vacant third slip.

Marnus Labuschagne, on one, wasn't so fortunate.

He poked at an Ebadot ball outside off stump and edged to Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto at second slip, leaving Australia 61-3.

Cameron Green came in and played some big shots before chipping Taskin to short midwicket, where Mushfiqur Rahim took an easy catch.

Wicketkeeper Alex Carey looked in good touch after lunch and cruised to 19 until he played on to Ebadot with the score on 129.

Taskin then produced the ball of the day to beat Beau Webster's bat and clip the top of off stump to leave the home side struggling on 152-6.

Cummins tried to steer the hosts to tea without further loss, however Shanto brought Hasan back into the attack with immediate success, the Australian skipper getting a big edge to Litton.

Hasan got his fourth in the same fashion, Mitchell Starc getting a thin edge to the keeper with the score on 172.

Smith threw his wicket away going for a big hit before Nathan Lyon was last man out in similar fashion.

item.title: Total darkness, then sunset as full eclipse wows spectators in Spain
item.description:
SOLAR-ECLIPSE/SPAIN

  • Up to 6 million visitors gather across eclipse path in Spain

  • Spanish authorities step up security amid wildfire concerns

  • Iceland estimates 80,000 visitors

  • Dedicated eclipse chasers seek clear skies

Spectators across Spain watched in wonder, some whipping off their protective glasses and rising to their feet in unison, as a rare total solar eclipse swept across the north of the country on Wednesday evening, plunging it into darkness.

Spain deployed a massive police contingent and set up special viewing spots across rural areas that offered the best views of the spectacle.

Viewers in Buitrago de Lozoya, a rural district north of Madrid, clapped and cheered as the sky dimmed and Baily’s beads - bright points of sunlight that shine around the edge of the moon during a total eclipse - glistened on the horizon just after 8:30 p.m. (1830 GMT), lasting barely a minute.

“It’s impressive how the colours return little by little after totality - first the reds, then the blues - just like at dawn and sunset, totally deceiving your brain,” said economist Diego Fernandez, 32.

Rafael Jiménez, 50, a resident of Madrid, said the event felt like science fiction. “It was an absurd scene; we even got soaked when the garden sprinklers kicked in,” he said. “And then, just like that, we were watching the sunset again.”

Spain’s turn with the eclipse followed shortly after a less remarkable spectacle over much of overcast Iceland, although a break in the clouds in the far west of the Nordic country allowed holidaymakers and locals a glimpse of the celestial phenomenon. The eclipse was hidden behind clouds in central Reykjavik although the darkness of the totality was still evident.

“It was like a whole day just came at once and I felt goosebumps because it just made us think about ... the shortness of life, how time can be different and it depends on your perspective,” lawyer Eduarda Ortiz, 33, told Reuters in the Icelandic capital.

Millions of people gathered in Iceland and northern Spain to witness Western Europe’s first total solar eclipse in 27 years.

Brian May, former guitarist for the rock band Queen, was among them. He travelled to an observatory in Spain’s Teruel province and chronicled the experience on his Instagram page.

“Here we go, the sun is disappearing. It’s amazing,” he said as the eclipse reached its climax and bystanders burst into cheers and applause after a countdown.

In Spain, authorities were expecting up to 6 million visitors in mostly rural areas under the eclipse’s path across the north of Spain and the Balearic Islands.

Police, planes and helicopters on standby

The Iberian Peninsula last witnessed a total solar eclipse in 1912, but another is due on 2 August 2027, and an annular eclipse will follow in January 2028, completing the so-called “Iberian Eclipse Trio”.

The uncanny sensation when day briefly turns to twilight and some animals fall quiet, while the moon passes directly between Earth and the sun, has often been seen through history as an omen of cosmic struggle or a sign of divine power.

For Spain, the event has been a chance to showcase its less-travelled regions and draw tourists from its overcrowded beach resorts. Some seized the opportunity to get married, according to local press reports.

The eclipse took place in one of the country’s highest-risk periods for wildfires, with emergency crews fighting various fires on Wednesday, including a large one in the southern Andalucia region.

Authorities rolled out a large-scale police operation and public safety campaign to make sure the crowds did not set off wildfires.

A small fire erupted near an eclipse viewing point in the town of Peñíscola, in the Valencia region, local authorities said. The fire began in a vehicle and spread to 33 more before firefighters brought it under control, they said. Emergency crews, including aircraft, were dispatched to the area.

The authorities dispatched 25,000 police officers to guarantee security around the eclipse observation sites and deployed nearly 100 planes and helicopters.

As of late Wednesday, no wildfire incident tied to eclipse chasers was reported.

Eclipse fever in the land of sagas

In Reykjavik, glasses that allow spectators to view the phenomenon without damaging their eyes have been sold out for days, as the country of roughly 400,000 people welcomed up to 80,000 visitors.

Totality reached Iceland’s westernmost coast at about 5:44 p.m. (1744 GMT), casting the far west of the island nation into total darkness for up to 2 minutes and 13 seconds.

The event has drawn both casual observers and “eclipse chasers”, enthusiasts who crisscross the globe to be in the path of totality whenever and wherever an eclipse occurs.

In Spain, 43-year old Gema, who did not give her last name, said as she left the Buitrago de Lozoya viewing point: “Everybody tells you about it, but it is more beautiful than you imagine.”

item.title: July Uprising Memorial Museum Act: 10 years' imprisonment for damaging artefacts
item.description:
"July Mass Uprising Memorial Museum Act, 2026" has been enacted to establish and operate the July Mass Uprising Memorial Museum.
Under the law, any person causing damage to any immovable artefact of the July Mass Uprising Memorial Museum will be punishable with up to 10 years' imprisonment, a fine of up to Tk10 lakh, or both.
The law was enacted on April 10, 2026, to establish and operate the museum for preserving, researching and displaying the history, artefacts and documents relating to the July-August 2024 mass uprising and the anti-autocracy movement.
The July Mass Uprising Memorial Museum, established under the law to preserve the memories of the 2024 mass uprising, was inaugurated by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on August 5. The historic museum was formally opened to the public the following day.
Section 4 of the Act states that the museum's head office will be located at Ganabhaban in Dhaka. The museum will also have the authority to declare, preserve and maintain secret detention centres where crimes against humanity were committed during the rule of the fascist government from January 1, 2009, to August 5, 2024.
If any such secret detention centre is under the control of an organisation, the organisation will be required to hand it over to the museum in its existing condition.
The detention centres linked to crimes against humanity will be considered and operated as branch museums of the July Mass Uprising Memorial Museum.
According to Section 5, the functions of the museum include searching for, collecting, preserving, researching and displaying historical artefacts and memorabilia related to the July Mass Uprising and the fall and flight of the fascist government; artefacts related to the history of East Bengal, the Language Movement, the struggle for independence and the 1971 Liberation War; and memorabilia, documentary evidence and other objects related to anti-democratic and anti-human rights activities and the rise of fascism.
Section 15 states that, with recommendations from the board and prior government approval, the museum may permanently or temporarily exchange July uprising artefacts with the Bangladesh National Museum or any other museum or individual for display and preservation. It may also give or receive such artefacts as gifts. Such permanent or temporary exchanges, as well as giving or receiving gifts, will require agreements.
Section 16 provides that if there are reasonable grounds to believe that any July Uprising-related artefact is in the possession of any person or organisation, the Director General or an authorised employee may inspect the place concerned and take appropriate measures in accordance with the Act or rules and regulations made under it.
Regarding access to the museum, Section 17 states that members of the public will be allowed to enter the museum upon payment of an admission fee determined by the board.
Section 22 provides penalties for destroying or damaging immovable artefacts. Any person who destroys, damages, alters or causes damage to any immovable artefact of the museum, or any part thereof, will be considered to have committed an offence and will be punishable with up to 10 years' imprisonment, a fine of up to Taka 10 lakh, or both.
Under Section 23, stealing, smuggling, destroying, damaging or altering any movable artefact of the museum will constitute an offence punishable with up to five years' imprisonment, a fine of up to Taka 5 lakh, or both.
Meanwhile, Section 24 states that engraving, writing, inscribing or putting a signature on any collected or registered artefact of the museum will constitute an offence punishable with up to one year's imprisonment, a fine of up to Taka 10,000, or both.
Section 25 provides that if any officer or employee of the museum is accused of any of the offences mentioned above, departmental proceedings may be initiated against them for misconduct in addition to the prescribed punishment. In such cases, caution must be exercised in reaching a final decision while proceedings are pending before a court.

item.title: Gold jewellery price hiked by Tk1,633 per bhori
item.description:
The price of gold jewellery has increased again in Bangladesh, with the Bangladesh Jewellers Association (Bajus) raising the price of 22-carat gold by Tk1,633 per bhori.
Under the new rates, a bhori (11.664 grams) of 22-carat gold jewellery will cost Tk236,779, including VAT.
The price adjustment was made in response to an increase in the price of pure gold in the local market. The new rates came into effect at 10am on Thursday.
The decision was taken at a meeting of the Bajus Standing Committee on Pricing and Price Monitoring. The new rates were announced in a notification signed by committee Chairman Dr Dewan Aminul Islam Shaheen.
According to the new rates, 22-carat hallmarked gold costs Tk20,300 per gram, while 21-carat gold is priced at Tk19,390 per gram and 18-carat gold at Tk16,650 per gram. Traditional gold is priced at Tk13,600 per gram.
Bajus has also revised the prices of silver jewellery.
Under the new rates, 22-carat hallmarked silver costs Tk435 per gram, 21-carat Tk415 and 18-carat Tk360. Traditional silver is priced at Tk270 per gram.
Bajus said labour charges will be added based on the design and type of jewellery. However, as VAT is included in the announced selling prices, it cannot be charged separately from customers.
The association also said its existing rules on the exchange and sale of old gold and silver jewellery will remain in effect, excluding applicable VAT, labour and stone charges.
The new prices will remain effective at jewellery shops across the country until further notice.
Bajus has revised gold prices several times in recent months amid fluctuations in international and local markets. The repeated price hikes have put gold increasingly out of reach for ordinary buyers, particularly those purchasing it for weddings, social occasions or as a form of savings.
